issues.legal_issue: A divorced spouse who claims a right to occupy a rented home through a former spouse is not entitled to be added as a party to the landlord’s eviction suit when the former tenant is contesting the suit and the divorce arrangements make no provision for the spouse’s residence in the home.
material_facts: The suit was brought by the landlady to evict the recorded tenant on grounds including unauthorised subletting.

The appellant was divorced from the recorded tenant. The divorce order, made by mutual consent, provided maintenance for the minor children only and made no provision for the appellant’s residence in the tenanted premises.
The recorded tenant was alive, had filed a written statement, and was contesting the eviction suit.
The appellant had no contractual tenancy with the landlady and claimed her right to remain in the premises through her former husband and her role as custodian of their children.
The landlady’s letter described the appellant’s occupation as unauthorised and illegal pending completion of formalities; the Court held that it did not recognize her as a subtenant.
issues.conclusion: The appellant was neither a necessary nor a proper party under Order 1 Rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, and the courts below correctly rejected her application to be added as a defendant.
issues.legal_principle: Order 1 Rule 10(2) CPC permits addition only of a necessary party, without whom no effective order can be made, or a proper party whose presence is needed for complete and final adjudication. Under B.P. Achala Anand v. S. Appi Reddy, a divorced spouse’s right to residence in a tenanted matrimonial home depends on the divorce arrangements, including whether residence was provided for; the spouse’s rights cannot exceed those of the tenant. The Court also applied the distinction between necessary and proper parties stated in Balvant N. Viswamitra v. Yadav Sadashiv Mule and relied on Razia Begum v. Sahebzadi Anwar Begum regarding the discretionary exercise of the joinder power. Sections 3(b), 18 and 23 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 define and address maintenance, including residence; Section 25 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 concerns permanent alimony and maintenance. The Court found that the divorce order provided maintenance for the children only and did not provide residence for the appellant.

rule.if: eviction_suit and proposed_party_is_divorced_former_spouse and divorce_order_provides_support_only_for_children and tenant_is_alive_and_contesting and (no_contractual_tenancy_with_landlord and claims_occupation_through_former_spouse)

predicates.eviction_suit: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction of the recorded tenant.
predicates.proposed_party_is_divorced_former_spouse: The person seeking to join the proceeding was divorced from the recorded tenant.
predicates.divorce_order_provides_support_only_for_: The divorce arrangements provided support for the children but did not provide the former spouse residence in the rented home.
predicates.tenant_is_alive_and_contesting: The recorded tenant was alive and actively contesting the eviction proceeding.
predicates.no_contractual_tenancy_with_landlord: The person seeking to join was not a party to a tenancy agreement with the landlord.
predicates.claims_occupation_through_former_spouse: The person seeking to join based the claimed right to occupy the home on the former spouse’s tenancy.

issues.definition: When an eviction proceeding is brought against a tenant, a divorced former spouse whose divorce arrangements provide support only for the children, who has no tenancy agreement with the landlord, and whose occupancy claim is through the former spouse is not added when the tenant is alive and contesting the proceeding.
